paragraphs.text: For most of the history of agriculture, farmers did not buy their seed; they kept it. After each harvest, the best heads of wheat or the healthiest beans were set aside for the following season, and over thousands of years this quiet selection produced an enormous range of local types, each suited to a particular soil, climate or taste. During the twentieth century, much of that variety began to disappear. As high-yielding modern varieties spread, farmers in many regions abandoned the older types their families had grown for generations, and once a variety is no longer planted, it can vanish within a few seasons. Seed banks were established largely in response to this loss.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The value of old varieties is not merely historical. Plant breeders depend on genetic variation, and the traits they need most urgently, such as tolerance of drought, heat or salty soil, or resistance to a newly arrived disease, are often found not in modern crops but in traditional varieties and in the wild species from which crops were domesticated. These wild relatives have survived for millennia without human care, and many carry genes that domestication left behind. Yet they are themselves under threat, since they tend to grow at field edges, on roadsides and in grasslands that are easily ploughed or built on. For this reason, many conservationists regard collecting their seed as no less urgent than preserving farmers' varieties.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A seed bank is, at its simplest, a cold store combined with careful record-keeping. When a sample arrives, usually gathered by a collecting team that has noted exactly where and when the plants were found, the seeds are first cleaned of chaff and soil and inspected for damage or insects. They are then dried slowly until only a small fraction of their weight is water. Moisture is the main enemy of a stored seed: if too much remains, ice crystals form when the seeds are frozen and burst their cells. Finally, the seeds are sealed in airtight foil packets or glass jars and placed in rooms kept at around minus eighteen degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many grain crops can remain alive for decades, and some may last for centuries.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Storage, however, is not the end of the process. Even in a freezer, seeds slowly age, so staff remove a few seeds from each sample at regular intervals and attempt to germinate them. If the proportion that sprouts falls below an agreed level, the sample must be regenerated: it is planted out, grown to maturity and harvested to produce fresh seed. This step is costly and surprisingly risky. A study led by agronomist Lena Marsh, which examined decades of records from a large national collection, found that regeneration plots of crops such as maize, whose flowers are pollinated by wind, frequently received pollen from neighbouring plants, so the new seed no longer matched the original sample. Marsh concluded that separating plots by distance, although expensive, was essential.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Because any single building can be damaged by war, flood or simple mismanagement, collections are commonly duplicated elsewhere. The best-known backup facility is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, cut into a mountainside on a Norwegian island far inside the Arctic Circle, where the surrounding permafrost would keep the samples cold even if the electricity failed. Deposits there remain the property of the institutions that sent them, and the vault's staff do not open the boxes. The arrangement proved its worth in 2015, when a research centre whose gene bank near Aleppo had been disrupted by the conflict in Syria withdrew copies of its own samples in order to rebuild its working collection elsewhere.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Not every plant, however, can be protected in this way. Many species, including cocoa, coconut and numerous tropical trees, produce what botanists call recalcitrant seeds, which die if they are dried and therefore cannot be frozen by the usual method. Other crops, such as bananas and potatoes, are normally grown not from seed but from shoots or tubers, and most cultivated bananas produce no viable seed at all. These must be maintained as living plants in field collections, as tiny plantlets in test tubes, or by cryopreservation, in which small pieces of tissue are stored in liquid nitrogen at far lower temperatures than an ordinary seed bank uses.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: A deeper criticism concerns what a seed bank cannot preserve. A sample stored in 1980 reflects the conditions of 1980; while it waits in the freezer, the pests, diseases and climate outside continue to change. The ecologist Tomás Ferreira argues that populations growing in farmers' fields and in the wild keep adapting, and that conservation on farms and in protected habitats should be treated as a partner to seed banks rather than an old-fashioned alternative. He adds that a stored seed arrives without the knowledge of how it was grown, cooked or valued, which survives only in the communities that cultivated it. Seed banks, in this view, are an indispensable insurance policy, but not a replacement for living diversity.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Saving Seeds for Tomorrow's Harvests

A. For most of the history of agriculture, farmers did not buy their seed; they kept it. After each harvest, the best heads of wheat or the healthiest beans were set aside for the following season, and over thousands of years this quiet selection produced an enormous range of local types, each suited to a particular soil, climate or taste. During the twentieth century, much of that variety began to disappear. As high-yielding modern varieties spread, farmers in many regions abandoned the older types their families had grown for generations, and once a variety is no longer planted, it can vanish within a few seasons. Seed banks were established largely in response to this loss.

B. The value of old varieties is not merely historical. Plant breeders depend on genetic variation, and the traits they need most urgently, such as tolerance of drought, heat or salty soil, or resistance to a newly arrived disease, are often found not in modern crops but in traditional varieties and in the wild species from which crops were domesticated. These wild relatives have survived for millennia without human care, and many carry genes that domestication left behind. Yet they are themselves under threat, since they tend to grow at field edges, on roadsides and in grasslands that are easily ploughed or built on. For this reason, many conservationists regard collecting their seed as no less urgent than preserving farmers' varieties.

C. A seed bank is, at its simplest, a cold store combined with careful record-keeping. When a sample arrives, usually gathered by a collecting team that has noted exactly where and when the plants were found, the seeds are first cleaned of chaff and soil and inspected for damage or insects. They are then dried slowly until only a small fraction of their weight is water. Moisture is the main enemy of a stored seed: if too much remains, ice crystals form when the seeds are frozen and burst their cells. Finally, the seeds are sealed in airtight foil packets or glass jars and placed in rooms kept at around minus eighteen degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many grain crops can remain alive for decades, and some may last for centuries.

D. Storage, however, is not the end of the process. Even in a freezer, seeds slowly age, so staff remove a few seeds from each sample at regular intervals and attempt to germinate them. If the proportion that sprouts falls below an agreed level, the sample must be regenerated: it is planted out, grown to maturity and harvested to produce fresh seed. This step is costly and surprisingly risky. A study led by agronomist Lena Marsh, which examined decades of records from a large national collection, found that regeneration plots of crops such as maize, whose flowers are pollinated by wind, frequently received pollen from neighbouring plants, so the new seed no longer matched the original sample. Marsh concluded that separating plots by distance, although expensive, was essential.

E. Because any single building can be damaged by war, flood or simple mismanagement, collections are commonly duplicated elsewhere. The best-known backup facility is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, cut into a mountainside on a Norwegian island far inside the Arctic Circle, where the surrounding permafrost would keep the samples cold even if the electricity failed. Deposits there remain the property of the institutions that sent them, and the vault's staff do not open the boxes. The arrangement proved its worth in 2015, when a research centre whose gene bank near Aleppo had been disrupted by the conflict in Syria withdrew copies of its own samples in order to rebuild its working collection elsewhere.

F. Not every plant, however, can be protected in this way. Many species, including cocoa, coconut and numerous tropical trees, produce what botanists call recalcitrant seeds, which die if they are dried and therefore cannot be frozen by the usual method. Other crops, such as bananas and potatoes, are normally grown not from seed but from shoots or tubers, and most cultivated bananas produce no viable seed at all. These must be maintained as living plants in field collections, as tiny plantlets in test tubes, or by cryopreservation, in which small pieces of tissue are stored in liquid nitrogen at far lower temperatures than an ordinary seed bank uses.

G. A deeper criticism concerns what a seed bank cannot preserve. A sample stored in 1980 reflects the conditions of 1980; while it waits in the freezer, the pests, diseases and climate outside continue to change. The ecologist Tomás Ferreira argues that populations growing in farmers' fields and in the wild keep adapting, and that conservation on farms and in protected habitats should be treated as a partner to seed banks rather than an old-fashioned alternative. He adds that a stored seed arrives without the knowledge of how it was grown, cooked or valued, which survives only in the communities that cultivated it. Seed banks, in this view, are an indispensable insurance policy, but not a replacement for living diversity.
